DIRECTION A · SIGNAL

Editorial dark. Large serif name, generous space, one warm accent, monospace micro-labels for the technical texture.

Why: reads senior and considered — closest to a personal site, furthest from a CV template. The writing carries the page.

Tradeoff: less immediately "technical" at a glance. Needs the copy to be strong, which yours now is.

DIRECTION B · CONSOLE

Engineering-forward. Monospace throughout, faint grid, numbered bullets, sharp green accent, terminal cues used lightly.

Why: signals "infrastructure person" in the first second. A technical lead recognises themselves in it.

Tradeoff: the terminal metaphor is polarising — some recruiters read it as junior/developer-y rather than senior.

DIRECTION C · CONTROL ROOM

Systematic and dense. Fixed sidebar nav, panelled sections, everything scannable without scrolling far.

Why: fastest to scan, and the structure itself argues that you build organised systems. Best fit for a busy recruiter.

Tradeoff: panel-and-sidebar is familiar territory — it has to be executed precisely or it reads like an admin template.

THE "VIEW PROGRAM" MODAL

Both routes you asked for: this panel opens in place with the coursework, and the footer still links out to the official university page.

Shown in Direction A's styling — it adapts to whichever direction you pick.

The Paris 8 list shown here is now checked against the real official syllabus (12 of 14 items confirmed verbatim). Two programs on the CV have NO official source at all and rest on memory only — Sorbonne Paris Nord's EID2 master and USTHB's "Master SII" — worth a personal sanity-check before those go live.
